title: Fresh starts
hook: people start new habits more often after a birthday, a Monday, a new month (Dai, Milkman and Riis)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the white bear, and the line not the bear. What did you put in the bear's seat when it came back? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

New Year's Day. A Monday. The morning after a birthday. The first day at a new job. On mornings like these, promises seem easier to make, and gyms seem a little busier. Three researchers, Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis, wondered whether that was real or just a feeling. So they looked at what people searched for online, how often people went to a university gym, and when people signed up to commit to goals. The pattern they found got a name of its own.
screen: `A MONDAY. A BIRTHDAY. A NEW JOB.` → `REAL, OR JUST A FEELING?` → `SEARCHES, GYM VISITS, GOALS.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. Searches for the word 'diet,' gym visits and goal commitments all rose after what the researchers called temporal landmarks: the start of a new week, a new month, a new year, a birthday, a holiday. They named it the fresh start effect. Second, the why. Their explanation is that landmarks draw a line in the story people tell about themselves. The person who skipped the gym belongs to last month. The new month seems to belong to someone a little different, and that bit of distance makes starting feel possible. Third, the honest edge. A fresh start is a moment to begin, not a promise of finishing. And there's a quiet trap in waiting for one: Monday becomes a reason not to start on Thursday. A landmark helps most when it's used, not waited for. Fourth, an old line about new mornings. The book of Lamentations, in the Hebrew Bible, is a book of grief over a ruined city. In the middle of it, the writer says of the Lord's mercies: 'They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.' Jews and Christians both read those words. They point to something the research also hints at. A fresh start doesn't need January. Every morning is already a small landmark, and so is this breath.
screen: `THE FRESH START EFFECT.` · `A LINE IN THE STORY OF YOURSELF.` · then, large: `USED, NOT WAITED FOR.` · then: `NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick your next fresh start. It can be large, like the first of next month, or small, like tomorrow morning, or the moment this sit ends. Pick one, and one small thing to begin there. Then let the plan rest, and spend the sit with the breath, treating each breath as a small fresh start of its own. The bell holds the time.
Fresh starts. People begin new habits more often after landmarks: a Monday, a new month, a birthday. Today's word.
Your line: a fresh start. Today, name the next landmark you'll use, even if it's tomorrow morning, and say what begins there. Then don't let it slide past. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: People who use the fresh start effect often tie a new practice to the next natural landmark, such as a Monday, the first of the month or a birthday, and treat each morning as a smaller one.

trapdoor: what you thought: new year's resolutions are just a cliché.
what it means: landmarks like a new week or a birthday really do make people more likely to start.
what a scholar hears: Dai, Milkman and Riis tied the effect to people distancing themselves from a past, imperfect self at landmarks.
